doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Trumpet influences and his own style
summary: He names Armstrong, Hackett, Spanier and Braff as influences, and says he no longer listens much to others and likes his own style.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Your own personal tastes of trumpet players — you were influenced by you mentioned a couple of guys, Bobby Hackett, and who was the other earlier —
Well first off there’s Louis Armstrong.

I mean the shake or the wobble that I have as a part of my style was really out of Louis, I mean from listening out of Louis and from listening to Louis. And the melodic part I think the combination of me playing the xylophone and seeing those chords [scats] and listening to Hackett and his weaving notes, so I think that’s part of my playing is that. The intensity of certain players, Muggsy Spanier and the beautiful intensity of Ruby Braff. Those are probably the strongest influences on me. I don’t listen that much anymore. I mean I feel like, I mean to the older style. I’ll listen to world music or classical music now as opposed to listening to jazz players. I’m not interested in going into the modern field. I’m too far along the way right now to mess around. And I’ve had a good success with my style. I like my style. So I don’t listen too much now to other players.
That’s an important statement. I like my style you said.

Well I’ve done a lot of listening. It isn’t a case of saying well this is me, I’m a natural born, I come with this style and so I’ve done a lot of listening and I actually occasionally listen to what’s being played today and I just, it’s lovely but it’s not me. So I feel very comfortable where I’m at.
